title: Word problem for the S-combinator
formal: Is convertibility of closed S-combinator terms decidable? Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the least set with \(S\in\mathcal{T}\) and \((uv)\in\mathcal{T}\) whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal{T}\). The sole rewrite rule, applicable inside any term context, is \[(((Sx)y)z)\longrightarrow ((xz)(yz)),\qquad x,y,z\in\mathcal{T}.\] Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that halts on every pair \(p,q\in\mathcal{T}\) and decides whether they are connected by a finite sequence of forward or backward applications of this rule?
why: The S-only fragment retains duplication and nonterminating behavior with just one combinator. Its word problem tests whether symbolic equality becomes decidable after removing the other primitives of combinatory logic, beyond the already-known ability to recognize normalizing terms.
status_note: The original RTA list and the 2023 primary Satellite account leave this convertibility problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 did not find a decision or undecidability theorem. Normalization results do not resolve this target; no exhaustive present-day certification is claimed.

progress.text: Waldmann proves decidability of whether a closed S-term has a normal form, as recorded in the original list and the later Satellite account.
The Satellite account explicitly retains decidability of interconvertibility as an open question.

sentences: Closed S-terms are finite application trees using only the combinator S.
The rule sends S applied to x, y and z to the application of xz to yz, and can be used inside any subterm.
The word problem asks whether two such trees are connected by finitely many forward or backward rule applications.
Normalization is decidable for this fragment, but the 2023 source still leaves general convertibility open.
A solution supplies a Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof covering nonnormalizing terms as well.

context_blocks.text: RTA Problem 97, attributed to Barendregt in 1975, asks for this exact word problem on ground terms built solely from S and application. Rule direction can be reversed during conversion, even though operational reduction has a forward direction.

The 2023 Satellite account reports decidability of normalization and of head-reduction termination for this fragment, but explicitly leaves interconvertibility open. It also distinguishes convertibility from equality of certain infinitary semantic trees.

source_consolidations.note: The S-only source distinguishes weak convertibility of closed terms from normalization and head-reduction termination. It also records that equal Berarducci trees need not imply convertibility, so that infinite-tree semantics alone does not decide the retained word problem.

definitions: A term is a finite ordered binary application tree whose leaves are all the one constant \(S\). Application is not associative; by convention \(uvw\) abbreviates \(((uv)w)\). There are no object-language variables, other combinator constants, lambda abstractions, types or infinitary terms. The letters \(x,y,z\) in the rule range over entire closed terms.

A one-hole context is built from a hole \(\square\) by repeatedly forming \((Ct)\) or \((tC)\), where \(t\in\mathcal{T}\) and \(C\) is a one-hole context. Write \(C[t]\) for replacing its hole by \(t\). A forward step is exactly \(C[(((Sx)y)z)]\to C[((xz)(yz))]\). Both appearances of \(z\) on the right are copies of the same finite tree.

Terms \(p,q\) are convertible when there exist \(m\geq0\) and closed terms \(t_0=p,\ldots,t_m=q\) such that, for each \(i<m\), either \(t_i\to t_{i+1}\) or \(t_{i+1}\to t_i\). This is the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of the contextual rewrite relation. No extensionality, eta law or identification merely by an infinitary semantic tree is added.

The two input trees are written explicitly, for example using prefix encodings \(\operatorname{enc}(S)=0\) and \(\operatorname{enc}(uv)=1\operatorname{enc}(u)\operatorname{enc}(v)\) with a delimiter between the two trees. A decider is one deterministic Turing machine halting on all valid pairs and outputting yes exactly on convertible pairs; malformed descriptions can be rejected. No time bound and no normalization promise are imposed.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for all pairs of closed S-terms under this conversion relation, or a Lean-checked proof of undecidability. Deciding whether individual terms have normal forms, deciding only pairs of normalizing terms, or comparing a coarser semantic invariant is insufficient.

statement_review.notes: Recovered the exact ground S-only syntax and contextual weak-combinator conversion relation. Defined finite tree encoding, arbitrary subterm rewriting, bidirectional finite conversion, absence of additional equality axioms, and total decidability without a normalization promise. Preserved the consolidated Satellite source and separated its normalization result from the unresolved word problem.
